title: Shakti as a philosophy
hook: a poet about to write a long poem asks for one thing first: that his words and their meanings stay together

segments.voice: Yesterday, Shakti as a philosophy in the Devi Upanishad: the gods asked who are you, and the goddess answered, of the nature of Brahman. Whose whole answer did you hear? Day one thousand eighty-eight.

A poet sits down to write a long poem about the kings of Raghu's line, one king after another. And the first thing he writes isn't about any king. It's about a word and its meaning. The poet is Kalidasa, whose Parvati this path met in the forest not long ago. Before he tells a single story, he bows to a couple. Not a king and queen. Shiva and Parvati. And he chooses one picture to say how close they are. Today: the goddess and the god, held together the way sound holds sense.
screen: `A LONG POEM OF KINGS.` → `FIRST: A WORD AND ITS MEANING.` → `HE BOWS TO A COUPLE.`

segments.voice: Here is the verse, in paraphrase. Joined like word and meaning, for the sake of understanding word and meaning, I bow to the parents of the world, Parvati and Shiva. First, the picture. Word and meaning aren't two things that happen to be in the same room. You can't have a word without meaning; it's just noise. You can't hand someone a meaning without some sign to carry it. They are two, and they are never apart. That is how close the poet says the goddess and the god are. Second, why he asks. The poet bows to them for the sake of understanding word and meaning. He's about to spend a whole poem putting words to work. So he asks the couple who are word and meaning to help his words mean something. It's a writer's prayer, and a clever one: the same image twice, once about God and once about his craft. Third, the parents of the world. Kalidasa doesn't call Parvati a helper or a shadow. Mother and father, both together, are where the world comes from. That fits what this week has been hearing: Shiva can't stir without Shakti; Uma names Brahman; nature and spirit both come from the goddess. Fourth, the image people know. In temples and paintings, Shiva and Parvati are sometimes shown as one body, half him and half her, divided down the middle: Ardhanarishvara, the lord who is half woman. The poet's word and meaning and the sculptor's single body say the same thing in two arts. In both pictures, Shakti isn't a second god beside the first. She's the other half of the same one.
screen: `JOINED LIKE WORD AND MEANING.` · `A WRITER'S PRAYER, TWICE OVER.` · `THE PARENTS OF THE WORLD.` · `ONE BODY: HALF SHIVA, HALF PARVATI.` · then, large: `TWO, AND NEVER APART.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: word and meaning. Sit, and let the breath slow. Choose one simple word that matters to you: home, mother, peace, a name. Say it once, silently. Then just watch what arrives with it: a picture, a feeling, a face. Say it again, slowly, and notice whether the sound and the sense come together, without being asked. Rest in that joining for the rest of the sit. If you pray, you can choose the name of the goddess, or Shiva, or the name you use for God. The bell holds the time.
Shakti as a philosophy. Kalidasa bows to Parvati and Shiva, the parents of the world, joined like a word and its meaning.
Your line: Shakti as a philosophy. Today, before you send one message, read it once and ask: do my words and my meaning match? Day one thousand eighty-eight.

howItsDone: The opening verse of Kalidasa's Raghuvamsha is learned by students of Sanskrit and recited as an invocation, and images of Ardhanarishvara, half Shiva and half Parvati, stand in temples dedicated to Shiva.

fork.setup: you're a poet about to write a long poem on a line of kings. what do you do first?
options: start straight in with the first king.
bow to Parvati and Shiva, joined like word and meaning.
fork.reveal: Kalidasa bows to the parents of the world, joined like word and meaning, so his own words will carry meaning.

original.note: Sanskrit: vagartha, word and meaning, joined: Kalidasa's picture of Parvati and Shiva.

trapdoor: what you thought: Shakti is Shiva's wife, standing beside him.
what it means: the poet says they are as close as a word and its meaning: two, and never apart.
what a scholar hears: Raghuvamsha 1.1, vāgarthāv iva saṃpṛktau vāgarthapratipattaye, jagataḥ pitarau vande pārvatīparameśvarau.
recall: a saying: Akka Mahadevi's short free poems

notes: Raghuvamsha 1.1 paraphrased: vāgarthāv iva saṃpṛktau vāgarthapratipattaye / jagataḥ pitarau vande pārvatīparameśvarau. 'Parameshvara' given as Shiva.
Kalidasa is called only 'a poet of classical Sanskrit' to avoid superlatives and dates.
Ardhanarishvara is not in the cited verse; it is a general description of the image. 'Half woman' for ardha-nārī is a gloss of the name; confirm acceptable under the etymology rule.
howItsDone's claim that Ardhanarishvara images stand in Shiva temples is general; Keeper to confirm.

Editor pass: the 'say tree' hook told the listener what happens in their head and called separating word and sense 'nearly impossible'; replaced with a hook that starts in the poet's opening and links back to Kalidasa's Parvati (day 1079). The closing 'Shakti isn't a second god' line is now framed as the two pictures' claim, not the narrator's; practice no longer tells the listener what they will notice.
